Variants.Content: It should be understood as a positioning node connecting Ghiscari cities, inland farmlands, and slave trade routes; specific city lords, armies, and battles are not fixed knowledge. Slaver's Bay's heat, dry seasons, stone cities, and class system affected the way anyone lived there; merchants, slaves, soldiers, and farmers all called the same city the same thing.
Entry Lazarsi Local families also relied on irrigation fields, brick kilns, harbors, caravans, and shipping along Slaver's Bay; if any road, well, or wharf failed, the cost would fall first on them.

Entry Lazarsi They will also recognize the accents, laws, and credentials of the Guise Coast; reputations can travel great distances from taverns, but true distances must still be measured by wheel, oar, or horse's hoof.

Entry Lazarsi If you can supply supplies, avoid danger, and find a guide, it is worth marking in your itinerary; if you don't have these three things, no matter how loud your family name is, it won't be able to save the lost.

The craftsmen use their hands to measure the stone walls, wooden beams, iron doors, tombs, and seams left by generations of repairs in Lazhaxi. The priests use rituals to continue the hierarchical order of the Ghis gods, the step pyramid, and the ancient city-state. A stronghold was therefore not just a lord's hall, but also a place where weddings and funerals, vows, labor and local memories recurred.

Entry Lazarsi They care about irrigation lands, brick kilns, ports, caravans, and shipping along Slaver's Bay. They also look at whether seeds are left after grain collection and whether the city gates are open in times of disaster. When people from afar see coats of arms, what they see is whether there will be food to eat tomorrow.
